headlines.title: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal
headlines.summary: The Emmy Awards will stream exclusively and free on Prime Video worldwide starting in 2027 under a six-year deal.
headlines.article_text: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video under six-year deal Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon's Prime Video will become the exclusive global home of the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal beginning in 2027. The Emmys will stream live and free in more than 240 countries and territories, with no Prime subscription required. The agreement ends the Emmys' long-running broadcast network rotation among ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Emmy statue is seen on the red carpet ahead of the 74th Emmy Awards at the Microsoft Theater in Los Angeles, California, on Sept. 12, 2022. Chris Delmas | AFP | Getty Images The Emmy Awards will leave its long-running broadcast network rotation for Amazon Prime Video in 2027 under a six-year exclusive global streaming deal, the e-commerce giant and the Television Academy announced on Tuesday. Under the agreement, Prime Video will stream the annual awards honoring the best in TV for free to all audiences, including nonsubscribers, in more than 240 countries and territories. Prime Video's rights to the Emmys will begin with the 2027 ceremony. NBC, owned by Comcast , aired the 2026 ceremony on Sept. 14. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior. The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994 , with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement. "Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year," he said. The decision to move the 70-plus-year-old awards show to streaming reflects a broader trend in a shifting media landscape as Americans continue to ditch broadcast and cable TV for streaming service subscriptions. Streaming services have pushed further into live events in recent years, securing entertainment and sports rights alongside broadcast networks, and even winning rights that were previously exclusive to networks. In December 2025, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal with Alphabet's YouTube and YouTube TV for media rights to the Oscars, taking over from ABC in 2029. Some 56% who knew about private credit headlines said there was no change in their view on alternatives, while 30% said it made them more cautious and 14% said their view was more positive. Goldman surveyed 1,000 U.S.-based high-net-worth investors, who have at least $1 million of investable assets, and ultra-high-net-worth investors, who have at least $30 million of investable assets. headlines.article_text: Meta joins companies to tame ‘chaos’ of doing business with AI bots Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Walmart, Meta and OpenAI Chairman Bret Taylor’s startup Sierra are building a set of tech standards to make it easier to do business with AI bots. As Meta’s Muse and other buzzy AI agents like Instinct see a boom in popularity, some companies have struggled to figure out what's happening inside their walls. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists,” said Taylor. In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of the Facebook parent company Meta, takes the stage at the Meta Connect developer conference. Andrej Sokolow | Picture Alliance | Getty Images A month after Meta's launch of Muse, the personal agent that quickly turned into a viral sensation, a group of companies is coming together to try to simplify the process of bringing the technology into the business world. Meta, Walmart , Stripe and a handful of other companies are publishing what they're calling a "personal agent protocol." It's an open standard meant to dictate how artificial intelligence agents can interact with businesses. Enterprise AI startup Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, is part of the group. Taylor, who's also chairman of OpenAI and is leading the initiative, told CNBC in an interview that companies have a lot of work to do to figure out how and when personal agents are able to access information. "Companies will know when it's a personal agent versus an actual person. For a lot of companies there's a risk: you don't want just a random bot that isn't acting on behalf of a person to have access to this service," Taylor said. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists." Meta's Muse has become the most popular and buzzy version of personal AI agents since hitting the market in early September. It soared to the top of Apple's App Store and remains there, ahead of ChatGPT. However, Amazon is among the companies that have blocked Meta's agents, citing worries of website scraping. Amazon also blocked Perplexity's AI agent and sued the startup in November, alleging the company took steps to "conceal" its AI agents so they could continue to scrape Amazon's website without approval. Perplexity called the lawsuit a "bully tactic." For the new standard, Taylor compared it with the experience of logging into other websites with Google or Facebook credentials, technology he worked on when he was tech chief at Facebook. He said the practice will help with authentication so that businesses know if they're dealing with a bot, and will provide visibility into what personal agents are actually doing through these websites. David Singleton, vice president of engineering and consumer products at Meta Superintelligence Labs and former technology chief at Stripe, highlighted security. In order for agents to work well, he said, customers need to share credit card and personal information, and the new standard creates some level of visibility and control. "We're defining rails that we hope personal agents and business agents can run over for the future," Singleton said, comparing it to email. "If you think about email, it works great because it is a standard that everyone can use to talk to each other, and we think this is going to be quite similar." Singleton said Muse already has millions of users in the U..S and it's "growing rapidly." "What we're finding is that people love using Muse for all kinds of things, things like signing their kids up for classes, finding and buying the best gifts, scheduling that dentist appointment that you have been putting off for six months," he said. "We need a mechanism to have it go faster and smoother." While OpenAI and Anthropic aren't on board now, Taylor said he expects the AI giants to participate, and indicated he will be "really disappointed" if it's not being used by competitors. Memory chip stocks and ETFs — Seagate Technology slumped 9.1%, Western Digital tumbled 6.9%, Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) slipped 2.2% and SanDisk fell almost 2% as investors reassessed the outlook for demand and profits stemming from the data center boom. Artificial Intelligence plays — Ciena jumped 11.3%, Nebius Group climbed 9.5%, Astera Labs by 7.5% and CoreWeave was ahead 4% as enthusiasm returned Tuesday to stocks tied to the AI buildout. Moderna , Novavax — Both stocks pulled back, reversing some of the sharp gains made of late. Moderna traded 6% lower, while Novavax declined by 10%. Despite those declines, Moderna remained more than 130% higher over the past three months, while Novavax was up nearly 20% over that time. Vistra — Shares rallied 12% after the Energy Department unveiled a $4.2 billion nuclear investment in Pennsylvania and Ohio. The department said this "will deliver more reliable American energy, strengthen the grid, lower costs, and meet growing power demand." Marvell Technology — The chip company jumped after Marvell rolled out a rosy long-term revenue outlook at its Investor Day event. The company sees revenue in fiscal 2028 coming in at $20 billion, while analysts polled by FactSet sought $18.17 billion. The company also sees fiscal 2031 revenue in a range of $70 billion to $90 billion, compared to the consensus call for $47.04 billion. Lamb Weston — The producer of potato products saw shares rise more than 11%. Lamb Weston reported adjusted earnings of 75 cents per share on $1.67 billion of revenue in the first quarter, topping the FactSet consensus call for 59 cents a share and $1.65 billion. The company also lifted its fiscal year adjusted earnings per share to a range of $3.05 to $3.35 per share from its earlier call for $2.95 to $3.25 per share. Cybersecurity stocks — The Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) headed for a seventh consecutive winning day and hit another all-time high as investors snapped up cybersecurity names. Zscaler and Palo Alto Networks jumped around 3%, while CrowdStrike advanced close to 2%. Constellation Energy , Alphabet — Alphabet shares were slightly higher on the day, while Constellation Energy jumped 14%, after Google announced a major long-term power agreement with the power company. Google will buy power tied to 890 megawatts of new nuclear capacity, alongside a separate 2,700-megawatt supply agreement, supporting more than $4.3 billion in new Constellation investment. Option Care Health , McKesson — Shares of Option Care surged more than 30% following a report in the Financial Times that health care services company McKesson and private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice are in advanced talks to jointly acquire the infusion services provider in a transaction valued at more than $5 billion. McKesson stock traded marginally higher. Lennar , Berkshire Hathaway — In a regulatory filing, Berkshire Hathaway disclosed it purchased about 2.4 million shares of Lennar. The homebuilder gained nearly 4%, while Berkshire Hathaway was fractionally higher. Advanced Micro Devices — The chipmaker rose almost 4% after Citi raised its price target to $800, signaling more than 26% upside from Monday's close. The bank pointed to greater CPU demand, driven by Meta's Muse AI agent, for the target change. "AMD will be the primary beneficiary of the CPU renaissance," Citi said. Procter & Gamble — Shares of the household goods company rose 2.5% after Evercore ISI upgraded the stock to outperform from in line. The firm also raised its price target to $166, from $161 previously, implying about 14% upside from Monday's close. Corteva — Corteva shares surged 12% after JPMorgan upgraded the stock to overweight from neutral. It has a $19 price target on shares, implying 53% upside from Monday's close. The bank said Corteva's sharper focus on crop chemicals, along with improving agricultural commodity prices, should help drive the stock higher. — CNBC's Nick Wells, Scott Schnipper, Fred Imbert, Paulina Likos and Deena Zaidi contributed reporting

headlines.article_text: Trump says MAGA Inc. PAC to pay for TV ads that praised him Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Donald Trump said he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him and had been funded by the U.S. government. The White House later clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service ads moving forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which had run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election. A new Trump ad began airing on Tuesday. US President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 30, 2026. Jonathan Ernst | Reuters President Donald Trump said Monday evening that he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him, and which reportedly were funded from up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security . The White House later clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service ads moving forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which have run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election . Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress. On Tuesday a new ad paid for by the U.S. government began airing. It features clips of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussing the U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. "Nicolás Maduro had his chance ... until he didn't," Hegseth says in the ad. "He effed around and he found out." Another clip shows Rubio warning, "Don't play games with [President Trump] in office." The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately reply to CNBC's requests for comment on whether the super PAC would cover the cost of the new ad or whether the buy had already been placed before Trump's announcement and would remain taxpayer-funded. Critics say the ads mirror Republican campaign talking points. Another ads features images of Trump saying "America will never be a communist country." "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said. AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5. It's unclear if the new ad Tuesday was paid for by MAGA Inc. or taxpayers. Trump's announcement came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency." Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The Times said federal money to pay for the ads became available on Sept. 19, "when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department. Sen. Maggie Hassan , D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'" In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with." "They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," Hassan said. "There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account." On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called for the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate the ads. "The government is not the President's campaign committee, and the Treasury is not his campaign account. The federal government has no legitimate business billing the public for campaign messaging that a candidate's political committee should pay for," Schumer wrote in a letter . Last week, the advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint urging the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Trade Commission and TV broadcasters to stop airing the ads. Public Citizen previously asked the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate whether the ads violated federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act. That law restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. A White House spokesperson defended the ads in a statement in late September to CNBC, calling them "public service announcements" intended to remind "Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad." "The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country," the spokesperson said. MAGA Inc. has raised $424.4 million and spent $32.4 million during the 2025-26 cycle through Aug. 31, leaving the Trump Super PAC with $415.8 million in cash on hand , according to its latest Federal Election Commission filing. MAGA Inc. has spent at least $57 million this election cycle, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings, including $25 million in independent expenditures reported since the end of August.
